characters: Mr Adotey: a history teacher, in a dark shirt and plain tie, speaking gently.
Bernice: a 14-year-old girl in a school uniform, with a notebook and a serious face.
Efo: a 14-year-old boy in a school uniform, who always asks for evidence.
The school hall: a plain hall with benches and a banner for National Flood Disaster Day (story picture).

narrationPlan.voice: Quiet, steady voice for Mr Adotey; thoughtful young voices for the pupils
narrationPlan.pace: Slow, quiet and respectful; no rushing (about 115 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Very soft strings and distant rain; silence for the minute of remembrance (placeholder)
culturalNotes: 3 June is marked as National Flood Disaster Day. This story uses published accounts and an invented teacher and pupils. It names no victims and uses no graphic detail.
This is a painful subject. Teachers should be ready for strong feelings, and some learners may have lost family or friends in floods.
Numbers differ in sources and the story says so rather than choosing a figure.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?

Check against named sources: date 3 June 2015; floodwater carrying fuel; the fire at the filling station; death toll estimates of about 150 to more than 250; the flood and fire split being uncertain; National Flood Disaster Day; May 2025 rainfall of 132.2 mm with four or five deaths (sources differ); early June 2026 floods in the named areas.
Ask the school counsellor, NADMO or a community leader to review the wording and the safety advice.
Confirm that the story does not blame victims and that it does not include any identifiable real person.

teacherGuide.overview: A remembrance story for older learners. It tells a national tragedy with care, shows how experts handle uncertain numbers, and turns grief into three clear steps: our part, their part and staying safe.
learningGoals: Describe what happened on 3 June 2015 in a careful, respectful way.
Explain why a disaster has several causes.
Write a promise that includes both a personal action and a request to leaders.
beforeReading: Tell learners the story is about a real tragedy, that they may step out at any time and that a counsellor is available.
whileReading: At page 3, pause to discuss why we give a range and not a single number when records differ.
afterReading: Write a promise card and a short letter to an Assembly Member.
Make a safety poster about floodwater.
discussion: Why is it better to say “we do not know the exact number” than to pick one?
What can children do, and what must leaders do?
reflection: What would you want people to remember about a day like this?

mathsExtension.task: If one estimate is 150 and another is 250, what is the difference?
132 mm fell in three hours. How many mm per hour on average?

support: Provide sentence starters for the promise card: “I will… I ask leaders to…”.
stretch: Compare the 2015 flood with another disaster in another country and how it was remembered.

culturalNotes: 3 June is marked as National Flood Disaster Day. This story uses published accounts and an invented teacher and pupils. It names no victims and uses no graphic detail.
This is a painful subject. Teachers should be ready for strong feelings, and some learners may have lost family or friends in floods.
Numbers differ in sources and the story says so rather than choosing a figure.
localiseThis: Invite a local NADMO officer or Assembly Member to explain flood safety.
Hold a minute of silence only if it suits the school and learners.

whatWeKnow: A flood and fuel fire at Kwame Nkrumah Circle on 3 June 2015 caused a very large loss of life.
Flooding has recurred in Accra, including in 2025 and 2026.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: The exact number of people who died and how many died in the flood and how many in the fire.
The exact number who died in May 2025, which sources give as four or five.

factCheck.claim: On 3 June 2015 floodwaters carrying fuel reached a filling station at Kwame Nkrumah Circle where people had taken shelter, and the station exploded; estimates of the dead range from about 150 to more than 250; the split between flood and fire is uncertain; the day is now National Flood Disaster Day; flooding in 2025 and 2026 recurred.
factCheck.explanation: From a JoyNews feature on Accra’s flooding history, which flags the uncertain figures and says 132.2 mm of rain in May 2025 killed four people.
factCheck.reference: MyJoyOnline, “Accra under water again: inside Ghana’s 66-year flooding crisis that nobody has fixed”.

factCheck.claim: A May 2025 rain of 132.2 mm killed five people and displaced more than 3,000; the 2015 fire killed over 150 people; June 3 is National Flood Disaster Day.
factCheck.explanation: From an opinion article by an environmental policy lecturer, which differs from another source on the 2025 death toll (four or five).
factCheck.reference: Graphic Online, “Accra is not drowning by accident: why Ghana’s flood crisis demands more than drains”.

factCheck.claim: The Accra flooding killed more than ten people, including children, in a recent event; the disaster of 3 June 2015 claimed about 150 lives.
factCheck.explanation: From a Ghana News Agency feature.
factCheck.reference: Ghana News Agency, “Ghana’s flooding: women and children suffer needlessly” (4 July 2026).

pronunciation.guidance: Ghanaians often say "uh-KRAH" (stress on the second syllable).
"KWAH-meh". English speakers often say "KWAH-mee"; confirm the final vowel.
reviewerNotes: Confirm final vowel (meh vs mee) and the "kw" onset.
